faq.q: When is sargassum season in Tulum?
faq.a: The season runs April through September, peaking from May to July. November through March the beaches are usually clean, though stray patches can land at any time. Because each year is different, we track every beach with Copernicus satellite imagery refreshed when new satellite observations are available, so you see what is on the sand today rather than a historical average.

faq.q: Which Tulum beaches get the least sargassum?
faq.a: The ones that don't face due east: Playa Ruinas and Playa Santa Fe, sheltered by the bay and coastline shape, usually get less sargassum than Playa Paraíso or Playa Pescadores which face dead east. Playa Xcacel to the south also tends to stay cleaner. Check the live map: daily satellite data shows which beaches are seaweed-free right now.

faq.q: How reliable is the data on this site?
faq.a: We use the AFAI index — the same standard NOAA uses to detect floating sargassum from satellite — with Copernicus imagery refreshed when new satellite observations are available. Reports from people on the beach fill in what clouds can hide. Every beach shows the exact time of its last update and a confidence level, so you know how fresh the reading you're looking at really is.

faq.q: Can you forecast sargassum a week ahead?
faq.a: Yes, within reasonable limits. Sargassum drifts with the wind and currents, so once the satellite spots a mat offshore we can project its path toward each beach over the next seven days. Days 1 to 3 are the most accurate; days 4 to 7 show the trend. The forecast is recalculated every day with each new satellite pass.

faq.q: Do the hotels clean sargassum off their beaches?
faq.a: The resorts in Tulum rake their beachfront every morning, and many install offshore sargassum barriers. Even so, on a heavy landing day the seaweed comes back within hours. That's why it pays to watch the real satellite flow: if nothing new is inbound, a raked beach stays clean all day.

faq.q: What do I do if my beach is buried in sargassum?
faq.a: Move — the geography gives you options. If Playa Paraíso wakes up bad, Playa Ruinas or Playa Santa Fe are usually cleaner; Akumal and Xpu-Ha to the north are also good options nearby. With premium alerts we tell you the moment your beach changes status.

forecast.h1: Sargassum Forecast for Tulum — Next 7 Days
forecast.intro: Most sargassum forecasts for Tulum hand you one verdict for the whole town, built from official imagery that's already days old by the time it's published. This works differently: we run a separate forecast for each of the 5 beaches we monitor, because reality changes from one bay to the next — the same mat that buries Playa Paraíso can slide right past Playa Ruinas. Every morning the model ingests the latest Copernicus satellite pass, locates the mats drifting inbound, and projects landings for the next seven days, beach by beach. The result updates daily — four satellite reads a day feed it — so you can pick your beach day before the sargassum picks it for you.
forecast.method: We start from the AFAI (Alternative Floating Algae Index), the spectral signature Copernicus and NOAA satellites use to detect floating sargassum from orbit. Each detected mat is projected forward with wind and surface-current data — sargassum drifts at roughly 2.5% of wind speed plus the local current. For seaweed already on the sand we apply exponential persistence with a 3.5-day half-life: it decays unless fresh material arrives. Community reports correct the satellite when clouds get in the way. Accuracy is highest on days 1 to 3, and everything recomputes daily.

season.intro: Planning a Tulum trip and worried about sargassum and seaweed? Here's the honest 2026 picture — when the seaweed arrives, when the beaches stay clean, and how to time your trip. Short version: November through March is reliable and clean; the Atlantic belt arrives April through October, heaviest May to August. If your dates are flexible, that single fact plans the trip.
season.title: Tulum Sargassum Season 2026 — Month-by-Month Guide
season.desc: When does sargassum hit Tulum? April to September, peaking May–July. Month-by-month 2026 guide with daily satellite tracking.

months.text: The reliable window. Landings are rare and light, the Atlantic is at its annual minimum, and practically all of Tulum's beaches stay clean for weeks at a stretch. If avoiding sargassum is your priority, travel in these months.

The warning month. Satellites start picking up the first mats of the new bloom crossing the Atlantic. Beaches are mostly still clean, but stray patches can land on the open coast. Worth a glance at the map before you book tours.

The season kicks off. Landings become regular on the east-facing beaches — Playa Paraíso, Playa Pescadores — though still at moderate volumes that crews handle in the morning. Playa Ruinas, Playa Santa Fe and Playa Xcacel stay quieter.

The peak. The Atlantic sargassum belt delivers steady volume and the exposed coast can wake up buried several times a week. The gap between beaches becomes enormous: on the same day, Playa Paraíso can be brown and Playa Ruinas crystal-clear. This is when a per-beach forecast is worth its weight in gold.

Still strong but easing. Landings turn episodic: a beach can be covered Tuesday and raked clean by Friday. Resorts keep up the cleaning pace and sheltered beaches recover fast. The 7-day radar helps you dodge the pulses.

The tail of the season. Volumes drop week by week and by month's end most of Tulum's beaches are stably clean again. A late pulse can sneak in after a norte, so the cautious keep checking the map — but the odds are firmly in your favor.

season.tips: If your dates are flexible, book November through March and forget about seaweed. Traveling in peak season? Favor staying at Playa Ruinas or Playa Santa Fe — or pick a resort with daily cleaning and an offshore barrier. Check our map the week before you fly (last month's forum posts are useless), and once you're here, plan beach mornings and keep a cenote or a Cozumel day as your plan B for the heavy days.

beachBlurbs.tu001: Tulum's most famous public beach, with the Mayan ruins as a backdrop and iconic beach clubs. It faces dead east with moderate surf, so in season it's among the first to catch sargassum — each club rakes its stretch daily. Arrive early: you get the cleanest sand and the best spot under the palapa.
beachBlurbs.tu002: A traditional fisherman's beach with a more local vibe and fewer beach clubs than Paraíso. Fully exposed to the east, so at peak season it can wake up loaded. Cleanup depends on the hotels and restaurants along the stretch. On a clean day the water is a spectacular deep blue.
beachBlurbs.tu003: The beach right by the Mayan ruins: the most geographically sheltered stretch in Tulum. The bay formed by the ruins breaks some of the swell and the sargasso that hammers the open beaches. Calmer water, great for families, and the iconic Tulum postcard with the temple in the background.
beachBlurbs.tu004: A wide, long beach south of town, with boutique hotels and a quieter vibe than the northern hotel zone. Slightly more sheltered than Paraíso, so in season it often wakes up cleaner. Ideal for long walks and sunsets without the crowds.
beachBlurbs.tu005: South of Tulum, already in the Sian Ka'an reserve. White sand, shallow water, and an almost wild vibe. Receives variable sargassum depending on wind, but the malecón stretch gets cleaned daily and, outside of cruise ship days, the beach is almost private. For travelers who want the Caribbean without the corridor crowds.

extraPages.title: Why Is There So Much Sargassum in Tulum?
extraPages.desc: Why is there so much sargassum in Tulum? It comes from the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt, pushed by currents and wind. Real causes and satellite map by beach, 4× daily.
extraPages.h1: Why Is There So Much Sargassum in Tulum?
extraPages.intro: There's so much sargassum in Tulum because the algae don't originate here: they arrive floating from the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt, an enormous band of algae that grows between Africa and Brazil and that ocean currents and easterly winds push all the way to the Mexican Caribbean. It's an oceanic phenomenon, not a local one, and that's why no hotel can stop it from arriving. The root causes stack up: more nutrients in the ocean (Saharan dust, river discharges like the Amazon), warmer waters, and currents that funnel the algae straight to the Quintana Roo coast. The amount changes every year, every week, and every beach. That's why we don't give you a single verdict: we track each Tulum beach with Copernicus satellite imagery refreshed when new satellite observations are available, with a 0–100 Beach Score and today's status. We're the satellite watching the sea while you sleep — we measure, we don't guess.

sections.h2: Where does the sargassum reaching Tulum come from?
sections.text: The sargassum invading Tulum comes from the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt (GASB), a massive band of floating algae stretching thousands of kilometers from the West African coast to the Gulf of Mexico. There the algae reproduce in the open ocean and, carried by the North Equatorial Current and the easterly trade winds, cross the Atlantic and enter the Caribbean from the south. The Caribbean Current funnels it toward the Quintana Roo coast, where it hits the east-facing beaches — from Playa del Carmen to Tulum. It doesn't originate off Tulum: it arrives from outside. That's why the flow changes day to day with the wind, and why we track it by satellite beach by beach instead of relying on a seasonal average.

sections.h2: Why is there more sargassum some years than others?
sections.text: The amount varies hugely year to year because it depends on how much algae the Atlantic produced that season, and that's driven by several factors that add up. More nutrients in the water — iron-rich Saharan dust blown over the ocean, and river discharges like the Amazon and Congo — make the belt grow more. Warmer water accelerates its reproduction. And the direction of the currents and wind each year decides how much of that algae ends up in Tulum vs. staying offshore. That's why one season can be light and the next record-breaking. Since last year doesn't predict today, what matters is the fresh data: check the live map and the 7-day forecast for your beach.

sections.h2: Why some Tulum beaches get slammed and others barely any
sections.text: Sargassum doesn't land evenly: geography decides. Beaches facing due east — Playa Paraíso, Playa Pescadores — catch the algae first because they're exposed to the Atlantic inflow. The ones tucked into bays or facing away from the inflow — Playa Ruinas, Playa Santa Fe, Playa Xcacel — mostly dodge it. That's why on the same day Playa Paraíso can wake up brown and Playa Ruinas be crystal-clear. Don't trust the rule of thumb: check today's status for each beach before you head out.

sections.h2: Is sargassum dangerous? What do I do if it shows up?
sections.text: Fresh sargassum floating or just washed up isn't dangerous to swim in. The problem shows up when it piles up and rots on the sand: as it decomposes it releases hydrogen sulfide (H2S), that rotten-egg smell that can irritate eyes, nose and throat in large, poorly ventilated piles. Not a cause for alarm on a raked beach, but best to avoid the rotting mounds. If your beach wakes up loaded, move: geography gives you options. Playa Ruinas, Playa Santa Fe, or Akumal to the north are usually cleaner. With premium alerts we'll tell you the moment your beach changes status, so you decide before you load the car.

sections.h2: Is sargassum dangerous? The rotten-egg smell
sections.text: Fresh sargassum floating isn't toxic and you can swim near it, though it's unpleasant. The problem arrives when it piles up on the sand and rots: as it decomposes it releases hydrogen sulfide (H2S), that rotten-egg smell that irritates eyes, nose and throat, especially in large mounds under the sun. Don't get between decomposing algae and stay away from dense piles if you have respiratory issues, same with small children and pregnant women. A beach raked early with no new landing is perfectly safe. If your beach woke up loaded, the healthiest — and most beautiful — thing to do is use the map to find a clean one today instead of staying next to the rot.
